target_year_over_year_context.explanation:
Both disclosures describe Citigroup's use of credit derivatives and other risk mitigants to hedge corporate credit portfolio risk, noting that mark-to-market results are reflected in Principal transactions. The 2025 disclosure (D169) explicitly includes the sentence regarding the ACL model exclusion found in the 2024 context (D203), but the core mechanism description (derivatives, partial/full term, asset sales, P&L impact) aligns directly with 2024 D201. D169 also contains the hedge feasibility sentence from 2024 D202.

The 2024 disclosure (D202) specifically details the policy of determining economic feasibility before hedging the remaining life of partial-term economic hedges. This exact policy is stated in the 2025 disclosure (D169) at sentence c_2025_7_P269_S002. D169 is the only 2025 disclosure in the group containing this specific text.

comparisons.peer_topic: Risk mitigation techniques for commercial credit portfolio
comparisons.peer_summary: The bank uses syndications, loan sales, hedging, and credit derivatives to manage the size and risk profile of its commercial credit portfolio, carrying these derivatives at fair value with changes recorded in other income.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citigroup and Bank of America utilize credit derivatives and other techniques to economically hedge credit risk within their commercial corporate credit portfolios. Citigroup explicitly employs partial and full term credit derivatives and outright asset sales, reflecting mark-to-market results in Principal transactions. Bank of America similarly uses credit derivatives, loan sales, and syndications to manage the size and risk profile of its commercial credit portfolio, accounting for these derivatives at fair value. A key difference is that Bank of America specifies that certain credit derivatives used for lending commitments do not meet accounting hedge requirements, whereas Citigroup's disclosure focuses on the economic hedging nature and income reflection without explicitly disqualifying hedge accounting status in the cited text.

sentences.text: As part of its overall risk management activities, Citigroup uses credit derivatives, both partial and full term, and other risk mitigants to economically hedge portions of the credit risk in its corporate credit portfolio, in addition to outright asset sales.
The results of the mark-to-market and any realized gains or losses on credit derivatives are reflected primarily in Principal transactions in the Consolidated Statement of Income.
We also utilize syndications of exposure to third parties, loan sales, hedging and other risk mitigation techniques to manage the size and risk profile of the commercial credit portfolio.
These credit derivatives do not meet the requirements for treatment as accounting hedges.

peer_results.rationale: The retrieved candidate (gs_2024_7_D326) discusses credit exposure on OTC derivatives arising from market-making activities and counterparty risk management (CVA, collateral), which is distinct from the target's topic of using credit derivatives to economically hedge credit risk in the corporate credit portfolio.

comparisons.peer_summary: Credit derivatives used in credit portfolio management activities do not qualify for hedge accounting under U.S. GAAP and are reported at fair value, creating an accounting asymmetry with accrual-accounted loans that causes earnings volatility not reflective of true credit exposure changes.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase use credit derivatives to economically hedge credit risk in their corporate/lending portfolios and report these derivatives at fair value with gains/losses flowing through Principal transactions. Citigroup states these results are reflected primarily in Principal transactions. JPMorgan notes that credit derivatives in credit portfolio management activities are reported at fair value with gains/losses recognized in principal transactions revenue. JPMorgan adds detail regarding accounting asymmetry, explaining that because the hedged loans are accrual-accounted while derivatives are marked-to-market, this creates earnings volatility not reflective of true credit exposure changes. Citigroup's disclosure does not discuss this accounting asymmetry or volatility impact.

sentences.text: As part of its overall risk management activities, Citigroup uses credit derivatives, both partial and full term, and other risk mitigants to economically hedge portions of the credit risk in its corporate credit portfolio, in addition to outright asset sales.
The results of the mark-to-market and any realized gains or losses on credit derivatives are reflected primarily in Principal transactions in the Consolidated Statement of Income.

The credit derivatives used in credit portfolio management activities do not qualify for hedge accounting under U.S. GAAP; these derivatives are reported at fair value, with gains and losses recognized in principal transactions revenue.

This asymmetry in accounting treatment, between loans and lending-related commitments and the credit derivatives used in credit portfolio management activities, causes earnings volatility that is not representative, in the Firm's view, of the true changes in value of the Firm's overall credit exposure.
